messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others

Vignette:
Sokha was forty-seven, a married park ranger who had spent most of his adult life working outdoors in a state park where the work was steady and physical and, most days, quietly routine. That stability had been shattered when his young child became suddenly and life-threateningly ill. He had brought the child to the hospital after a day that began with ordinary family life and ended with panic in a fluorescent-lit emergency department, where the smell of antiseptic hung in the air and staff moved briskly between rooms while he tried to understand what was happening. He remembered the child looking small against the bed rails, the monitor sounds, and the strange unreality of being told that things were serious enough to require urgent treatment. What stayed with him most was the helplessness of that time, the sense that his attention had to stay fixed on every change in the child’s condition because something terrible could happen if he missed even a small sign.

Afterward, Sokha found himself reacting sharply to the most ordinary bodily sensations. If he felt dizzy or lightheaded, even briefly, his mind would go straight back to the hospital, and he would become tense and watchful, certain that the feeling meant something was wrong again. He noticed that the smell of hospitals or antiseptic could bring the whole period back in a rush, as if he were once more standing in that corridor trying to catch the eye of a nurse. The smell of alcohol had become just as powerful for him, not because it was part of his everyday life before, but because it now carried the same sharp, clinical association; if he passed someone using hand sanitizer or encountered the smell in a store, he would feel a jolt of dread and a tightening in his chest, and he would want to get away. These reactions were especially hard for him because his work as a park ranger sometimes required him to accompany visitors, give first aid, or deal with minor injuries, and he had come to dread situations where a person might mention a clinic, a hospital, or even a bottle of disinfectant in a backpack. In those moments he often became preoccupied with getting out of earshot or changing the subject quickly, as if avoiding the reminder could keep the memory from taking hold of him again.

Over time Sokha also began spending long stretches replaying the event in his mind, turning it over with a harsh, restless logic. He would dwell on what other people had done to him during that period, especially the sense that others had not understood how serious it was until he was already overwhelmed. At other times the rumination became more vengeful in tone; he would imagine how he might get even with the people he felt had wronged or failed him, though the target of that anger shifted depending on what he was thinking about at the moment. These thoughts did not leave him feeling settled. Instead, they kept him emotionally tied to the episode, returning him again and again to the unfairness of what had happened and to the humiliating feeling of having had so little control. He did not talk much about these thoughts, partly because he did not want to be judged and partly because being questioned about the event by others only intensified his distress. When friends or coworkers asked how his child was doing or tried to bring up the hospital period, he often shut the conversation down, changed the subject, or withdrew. He found such reminders hard to tolerate and preferred not to be reminded by anyone else, even people who meant well.

As the months passed, these reactions narrowed his world in quiet ways. At work he remained functional, but he had become more guarded in situations that might bring the memory close, and he was aware that he now organized parts of his day around not encountering certain smells or conversations. At home, he seemed preoccupied even when sitting with his wife, and she had noticed how quickly his attention could be pulled away by a dizzy spell or a whiff of alcohol-based cleaner. Sokha had finally agreed to seek help because he was tired of living as though he were still braced in that hospital corridor, waiting for another crisis. What he wanted most was to be able to be near his family and continue working without feeling ambushed by the smell of antiseptic, a moment of lightheadedness, or someone else’s well-meant question. What frightened him most was the sense that these reminders could still seize him as powerfully as they had at the hospital, and that he might never feel fully settled again.
